brief: Fidelity's Matthew Quaife (06/11/2026) frames the AI/semiconductor/data-centre sell-off as technical, not a thesis break. Cause: sweeping Democratic midterm wins, including Texas, Ohio and Georgia, raised regulatory and permitting concerns for data-centre construction, questioning the pace of AI capex; the move was amplified by crowded positioning, leverage and options hedging. Because this capex cycle runs on financing rather than consumer spending, a technical sell-off bites harder, and a capex slowdown could weigh on GDP growth and support bonds, which have already risen on hopes of calmer Middle East conditions. Near-term volatility should stay elevated, but technical oversold conditions historically create entry opportunities, and Fidelity still expects healthy earnings growth over the next two years with valuation compression making quality names attractive. Fidelity has trimmed and adjusted its AI/tech positioning, keeping it smaller and rotating toward AI adopters and higher-quality, easier-financed names. Away from AI, minimum-volatility and staples stocks have rallied (up more than 12% and 20% respectively since October) while broad indices are down over 2%, a rotation rather than a broad exit, partly hedge-fund-liquidation-driven; some of those defensive areas now look overbought. Fidelity's overall risk stance stays neutral, cut from overweight in September.
